subject: maths
title: Powers, roots and indices

slides.heading: Powers and roots — shortcuts for repeated multiplication
slides.body: A power (or index) tells you how many times to multiply a number by itself: 3⁴ means 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81. A root undoes a power: √81 = 9 because 9² = 81. These ideas appear throughout GCSE — in standard form, area, volume, and algebra — so the index laws are worth knowing cold.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: The index laws
slides.formula: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ | aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ | (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ | a⁰ = 1 | a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ
slides.formulaExplained: When multiplying powers of the same base, add the indices. When dividing, subtract the indices. When raising a power to another power, multiply the indices. Any base to the power zero equals 1. A negative index means take the reciprocal: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
slides.whenToUse: Whenever you multiply, divide or raise expressions that share the same base — the base must be identical before you apply any of these rules.
slides.note: Show formula in standard notation. Explain each variable. State when this formula applies.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: Simplify 5³ × 5² ÷ 5⁴, leaving your answer as a power of 5.

steps.instruction: Multiply the first two terms — same base (5), so add the indices.
Divide by 5⁴ — same base, so subtract the index.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Multiplying the bases as well as adding the indices — e.g. writing 3² × 3³ = 9⁵ instead of 3⁵.
mistakes.correction: When multiplying powers with the same base, keep the base and only add the indices: 3² × 3³ = 3⁵ = 243, not 9⁵.

mistakes.mistake: Multiplying indices when multiplying powers — e.g. writing 4² × 4³ = 4⁶ instead of 4⁵.
mistakes.correction: Multiply → add indices. The multiply-indices rule only applies when raising a power to a power: (4²)³ = 4⁶.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking that a⁰ = 0 — e.g. writing 7⁰ = 0 instead of 1.
mistakes.correction: Any non-zero base raised to the power 0 equals 1. This follows from the division law: aⁿ ÷ aⁿ = a⁰ = 1.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ — multiply powers of the same base by adding the indices.
keyFacts.examTip: The base must be identical. You cannot combine 3² × 5³ using this law.

keyFacts.fact: aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ — divide powers of the same base by subtracting the indices.
keyFacts.examTip: If the result is a negative index, e.g. 2³ ÷ 2⁵ = 2⁻² = 1/4 — do not write 0 or a negative number.

keyFacts.fact: (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ — raise a power to another power by multiplying the indices.
keyFacts.examTip: Distinguish carefully: 3² × 3³ = 3⁵ (add) but (3²)³ = 3⁶ (multiply). A common exam trap.

keyFacts.fact: a⁰ = 1 for any non-zero value of a. a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ — a negative index means 'take the reciprocal'.
keyFacts.examTip: 2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8. Write it as a fraction — never as a negative number.
